The figure, 36 positive results among 204 participants, carries a 95 percent confidence interval of 12.4 to 22.9 percent, and places the tested group in what the World Health Organization would classify as a high-endemicity setting, where surface antigen prevalence exceeds 8 percent. The study, published in the Springer Nature journal Discover Viruses, enrolled adults who presented to the hospital’s outpatient department with at least one clinical feature suggestive of viral hepatitis, such as jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, right upper quadrant pain, or hepatomegaly. All 204 eligible participants consented and completed the study, with no exclusions after enrollment. Because the investigators used consecutive sampling, every clinically suspected patient who arrived during the study window was recruited until the required sample size was met, a design the authors acknowledge may introduce selection bias and limit how far the findings generalize beyond this single referral center. Laboratory testing relied on the SNIBE Maglumi chemiluminescence immunoassay analyzer, which captures hepatitis B surface antigen from serum using magnetic microbeads coated with specific antibodies. After unbound components are removed by magnetic separation, an enzyme-labeled detection antibody is added, and the instrument measures light emitted when the enzyme reacts with a chemiluminescent substrate. The signal is proportional to the antigen concentration in the sample. Results were classified as positive when a cutoff index reached 1.0 or above, and borderline or equivocal readings flagged by the instrument were retested, with repeatedly reactive samples counted as positive. Daily internal and external quality controls were run, reagents were checked for expiration and storage conditions, and the analyzer was calibrated regularly. Discover more Check Symptoms Book Care Services Read Med Journals Compare Clinics Donate to Research Sample size was calculated in advance using a single population proportion formula, assuming a 95 percent confidence level, a 5 percent margin of error, and an expected prevalence of 14 percent drawn from a 2024 study at Guhalla Primary Hospital in Northwest Ethiopia. The initial calculation of 185 participants was inflated by 10 percent for anticipated non-response, yielding a final target of 204. Data collectors administered a structured questionnaire covering sociodemographic characteristics, behaviors such as alcohol use and sharing of sharp instruments, and medical exposures including blood transfusion, surgery, dental procedures, tattooing, and vaccination status. Venous blood samples of 3 to 5 milliliters were drawn aseptically with single-use needles and tubes. The participant group was evenly split by sex, with 101 men and 103 women. Nearly half, 98 people or 48 percent, were aged 25 to 34 years, while 58 participants, 28 percent, were 35 or older and 48, or 24 percent, were under 25. Clinically, 40 percent reported jaundice, 45 percent reported dark urine or pale stools, 48 percent reported fatigue or weakness, 43 percent reported right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and 32 percent reported nausea or vomiting. Behaviorally, 62 percent reported alcohol consumption within the past year, 45 percent reported sharing sharp materials such as razors, blades, or nail clippers, and 59 percent reported a previous sexually transmitted infection diagnosis or treatment. In bivariable analysis, three factors stood out. Participants aged over 35 had roughly three times the odds of surface antigen positivity compared with those under 25, with a crude odds ratio of 3.15 and a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.14 to 8.74. Jaundice showed the strongest crude association, with an odds ratio of 5.2 and a confidence interval of 2.34 to 11.54. Sharing sharp materials doubled the odds, with a crude odds ratio of 2.2 and a confidence interval of 1.05 to 4.60. After adjustment in a multivariable logistic regression model, four factors remained independently associated with positivity. Age of 35 years or older carried an adjusted odds ratio of 2.85, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.08 to 7.55 and a p value of 0.035, meaning these participants were roughly 2.9 times more likely to test positive than the youngest age group. Those aged 25 to 34 did not differ significantly from the reference group, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.90. Alcohol consumption was associated with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.52, a confidence interval of 1.13 to 5.63, and a p value of 0.037. A self-reported history of blood transfusion was associated with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.45, a confidence interval of 1.04 to 2.94, and a p value of 0.040, while sharing sharp materials yielded an adjusted odds ratio of 1.72, a confidence interval of 1.01 to 2.93, and a p value of 0.046. Discover more Explore Data Study Biology Get Health Tips Health health The authors are explicit that these associations should not be read as causal. The cross-sectional design cannot establish whether the measured exposures preceded infection, and with only 36 positive outcomes relative to the number of candidate predictors, the risk of model overfitting, unstable coefficients, and inflated effect estimates cannot be excluded. The transfusion finding in particular is treated cautiously: the study did not record when transfusions occurred, how many units were given, or how donor blood was screened, so the association cannot demonstrate that hepatitis B was acquired through transfusion. Alcohol consumption may likewise serve as a marker for unmeasured behavioral or socioeconomic factors, and residual confounding remains possible. Model diagnostics were nonetheless reassuring within their limits. Variance inflation factors peaked at 2.34 and tolerance values ranged from 0.43 to 0.89, indicating no substantial multicollinearity. The Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test produced a chi-square statistic of 8.14 with 8 degrees of freedom and a p value of 0.42, consistent with adequate calibration. No observation showed excessive influence, with Cook’s distance values below 1.0. The final model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.78, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.71 to 0.85, correctly classifying 75.0 percent of participants at the selected threshold, with 69.4 percent sensitivity and 76.2 percent specificity. A sensitivity analysis treating age as a continuous variable was reported in supplementary material. The 18 percent prevalence sits within a broader landscape of hepatitis B burden in the region. It is comparable to the 14 percent reported among clinically suspected patients at Guhalla Primary Hospital, to a 21.2 percent figure from Northern Uganda, and to a 17.6 percent estimate from Ethiopia, but lower than rates of 22.3 percent among chronic hepatitis patients and 28 percent among patients with chronic liver disease in prior studies. It is higher than community-based estimates, including 5.4 percent in a general Ethiopian sample and 9.0 percent among adults in another study, a gap the authors attribute partly to the symptomatic, hospital-recruited population studied here. Globally, an estimated 254 million people were living with chronic hepatitis B surface antigen positivity in 2022, with about 1.2 million new infections and roughly 1.1 million deaths. In Ethiopia, where surface antigen prevalence ranges from 6 to 12 percent and the infant hepatitis B vaccine was added to the routine immunization schedule in 2007, the authors call for strengthened screening, vaccination coverage, blood safety, and infection-prevention measures, and note that longitudinal studies are needed to clarify the temporal and causal relationships suggested by their cross-sectional findings. Researchers assessed 320 patients from October 2023 through January 2024, combining structured questionnaires, physical examinations and medical-chart reviews. HBsAg positivity, indicating the presence of hepatitis B surface antigen, was identified in 134 participants, giving a prevalence of 41.9% with a 95% confidence interval of 36.5% to 47.5%. The hospital-based design establishes the burden among people already receiving care for chronic liver disease, but it does not show whether hepatitis B caused their underlying liver disease or how common infection is in the wider regional population. The study focused on patients with established chronic liver disease, a group described in the research as vulnerable to acute or superimposed hepatitis B infection. The authors noted that such infections can trigger rapid hepatic decompensation, accelerate progression toward cirrhosis and increase the lifetime risk of neoplastic transformation. Its primary result was the prevalence of HBsAg positivity and the statistical associations between this status and reported or recorded characteristics. Multivariable binary logistic regression identified several characteristics associated with positive HBsAg status. HIV-positive participants had three times the adjusted odds of positivity compared with HIV-negative patients, with an adjusted odds ratio of 3.00 and a 95% confidence interval of 1.40 to 6.80. Discover more Study Biology Find Treatments Read Med Journals Soothe Digestion Check Symptoms A family history of liver disease was associated with 4.70 times the adjusted odds, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.90 to 11.00, while a history of dental procedures was associated with 4.50 times the adjusted odds, with a 95% confidence interval of 2.00 to 10.00. Contact with a person who had jaundice was also associated with higher odds of positivity, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.40 and a 95% confidence interval of 1.20 to 4.80. These are associations in the sampled population, not evidence that any listed exposure transmitted the virus. Because hepatitis B prevalence was high in the study population, the investigators also applied a modified Poisson regression model with robust variance to complement the odds-ratio estimates with adjusted prevalence ratios. In that model, HIV-positive status was associated with an adjusted prevalence ratio of 1.68, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.20 to 2.35. Family history of liver disease was associated with a ratio of 1.76, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.29 to 2.40. Contact with a jaundiced person had an adjusted prevalence ratio of 1.48, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.14 to 1.92, and a history of dental procedures had a ratio of 1.62, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.21 to 2.17. The logistic and modified Poisson analyses pointed in the same direction for these four predictors. Post-hoc power calculations indicated greater than 85% statistical power for the primary multivariable predictors. That calculation was performed after model fitting and does not eliminate uncertainties associated with the sample size, model specification, confounding or the cross-sectional design. In particular, the study cannot establish the timing or route of infection, determine whether identified characteristics preceded HBsAg positivity, or measure changes in prevalence over time. The referral-hospital setting also limits generalization: the participants were patients attending selected public facilities in Bahir Dar, rather than a population-based sample representing all people with chronic liver disease in Northwest Ethiopia. Discover more View Census Data Get Health Tips Book Care Services infection infections Within those limits, the 41.9% estimate documents a substantial hepatitis B burden among the chronically ill patients attending the three hospitals during the study period. The hospital sample included patients with chronic liver disease, so the result should not be presented as a regional prevalence estimate for the general population. Nor does the cross-sectional analysis demonstrate that HIV, family history, dental procedures or contact with a jaundiced person caused infection. The adjusted estimates identify groups with higher observed prevalence in this clinical setting, while their confidence intervals show the degree of precision around each association. The authors proposed that the results may inform regional planning for hepatitis B screening within liver clinics, evaluation of targeted adult vaccination strategies and stronger use of standard infection-control measures in health facilities. The immediate research contribution is instead a cross-sectional measurement of HBsAg prevalence and its reported correlates among 320 chronic liver disease patients in a defined Ethiopian hospital network. For interpreting the results, the study type and population are central. It was a facility-based, cross-sectional assessment conducted from October 2023 to January 2024, not a longitudinal study or a clinical trial. Its strongest supported conclusion is that hepatitis B infection was common among the sampled chronic liver disease patients, with HIV positivity, family history of liver disease, dental-procedure history and contact with a jaundiced person each associated with higher adjusted prevalence or odds of HBsAg positivity. The figure is a projection based on stated assumptions, not a count of actual infections. Researchers at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School built the model. The team followed a hypothetical group of 3.6 million babies born in the U.S. in 2026 through age 20, ABC News reported. Delaying the first dose until 2 months raised projected chronic infections by 19%. A shared decision-making approach raised them by 83% and left about 1.8 million young adults unprotected at age 20, compared with about 474,000 under a delayed dose and about 232,000 under a universal birth dose. For families expecting a baby, the finding lands on a real decision. Federal advice on the birth dose has shifted over the past year, and the guidance parents hear may depend on which hospital, pediatrician, or website they consult. Model Projections and Their Limits The study, described in a journal news release, used a Markov state transition model, a standard tool that moves simulated people through health states over time. It compared three approaches for babies whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B during pregnancy: a universal birth dose, a first dose at 2 months, and shared clinical decision-making. Results depend heavily on how many families end up vaccinating. In a scenario in which only about 26% of infants were vaccinated at 2 months, chronic cases rose 225%, TIME reported. The model also projected that perinatal infections could double or triple if babies of mothers who test positive, or whose status is unknown, became less likely to get the vaccine. The study does not prove that infections will rise by these amounts. It modeled a single year of births and relied on assumptions about vaccine uptake and infection rates. The researchers stressed that the numbers are simulation estimates, and real-world vaccination and infection data will be the true test. Dr. Amir Mohareb, an infectious disease researcher at Harvard Medical School and Massachusetts General Hospital and an author of the study, told TIME that the team "wanted to add some evidence to the conversation" about the possible impact of the changes. Two other recent modeling studies examined the issue. One found that delaying the first dose by 2 months would add about $16.4 million in health care spending on new infections, even if every child eventually received the vaccine. U.S. newborn hepatitis B vaccination rates fell from 83.5% to 73.2% between 2023 and 2025, according to an electronic health record analysis of 12 million infants. That decline began before the federal change took effect. Infancy is when the virus does the most lasting damage. About 90% of babies infected around the time of birth develop chronic hepatitis B, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics. Untreated infection early in life carries a lifetime liver cancer risk of about 1 in 4, TIME reported, and many people do not learn they are infected until liver damage appears years later. Kennedy Jr. has said his department puts informed consent, individual medical circumstances, and conversations between parents and doctors at the center of health decisions. Physicians worry that softer language changes behavior. Stanford pediatrician Dr. Alok Patel told ABC News, "When a recommendation shifts from 'every baby' to 'Let's discuss it,' a lot of families hear 'optional' or 'Maybe it was never that important.'" Babies born to mothers who test positive, or whose status is unknown, face the highest risk and should still get the vaccine within 12 hours of birth, according to the CDC fact sheet. records.content: ALBANY - An estimated 500 newborns received doses of the hepatitis B vaccine that had been improperly stored at Albany Medical Center in recent weeks, state and hospital officials said. State Department of Health workers discovered the error while reviewing refrigeration logs in preparation for a site visit to the hospital, agency spokesperson Marissa Crary told the Times Union on Thursday. The logs showed the doses had been stored below the manufacturer's recommended temperature range and may not have fully protected the babies who received them, Crary added. The improperly stored doses do not pose a health threat to the babies who received them, but their effectiveness may have been compromised. The concern is that the infants may not have developed the intended protection against hepatitis B, making repeat vaccinations necessary to ensure they are fully protected. Newborns typically receive their first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine shortly after birth, often before leaving the hospital. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends they receive a second dose within two months. Albany Medical Center sent a letter to affected parents and doctors informing them "that a repeat dose may be needed to ensure children remain fully protected," a hospital spokesperson said. It was unclear Thursday how many parents had brought their children back for a repeat vaccination. "We apologize for this situation and have implemented additional safeguards to help prevent it from happening again," the spokesperson said. State health officials will continue to oversee the hospital's "corrective actions," Crary said. The hospital is required to submit documentation showing it has remedied its vaccine tracking and temperature monitoring system. A Hepatitis B virus infection can cause serious liver conditions. School-aged children are required to receive three doses of the preventive vaccine. About 90% of New York children complete the three-dose series before the age of 3, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation. "New York state maintains vigilant programmatic oversight to protect patients and ensure hospitals provide safe, quality care," Crary said. There's more to Albany with the Times Union. SHOW MORE Nearly half of patients with chronic HBV or HCV also had MASLD, tied to worse fatigue and quality of life. Advertisement Roughly half of patients with chronic hepatitis B or C also have metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), and those carrying both diagnoses reported significantly worse fatigue, systemic symptoms, and quality of life than patients with viral hepatitis alone, according to a cross-sectional analysis of the Global Liver Registry published in the Journal of Gastroenterology and Hepatology.1 MASLD Adds to a Persistent Global Hepatitis Burden Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection remain among the world's most common liver diseases. An estimated 287 million people were living with chronic HBV or HCV infection in 2024, and the 2 viruses together caused roughly 1.3 million deaths that year, according to the World Health Organization's most recent global hepatitis report. Fewer than 5% of the 240 million people living with chronic HBV were receiving treatment.2 MASLD, driven by obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other cardiometabolic risk factors, has grown more common worldwide and increasingly coexists with viral hepatitis in the same patient. How that overlap affects day-to-day symptoms and quality of life, rather than liver histology alone, had not been systematically examined across a large, multinational cohort. A Global Registry Compares MASLD in Chronic Hepatitis The researchers analyzed cross-sectional clinical and patient-reported outcome (PRO) data from the Global Liver Registry, an international database of patients with chronic liver disease. MASLD was defined as a Hepatic Steatosis Index of 36 or higher plus at least 1 cardiometabolic risk factor (overweight, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, or hyperlipidemia). PROs were captured with the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy-Fatigue (FACIT-F) scale, the Chronic Liver Disease Questionnaire (CLDQ), and the Work Productivity and Activity Impairment questionnaire. The analysis included 4649 patients: 2063 with HBV (mean age, 48 years; 57% male; 11% with advanced fibrosis) and 2586 with HCV (mean age, 56 years; 47% male; 18% with advanced fibrosis). MASLD was present in 49% of the HBV group and 47% of the HCV group, underscoring how common the metabolic-viral overlap had become in this population. MASLD Worsens Fibrosis and Fatigue in HBV Patients with HBV and MASLD were similar in age, sex, and nonmetabolic comorbidities to those with HBV alone (all P > .05), but they had significantly more advanced fibrosis (P < .01). They also scored significantly lower on the FACIT-F Physical Well-Being and Fatigue domains and on every CLDQ domain (all P < .01), with the largest gap in the Fatigue domain, a 6% reduction across the scale's full range. That pattern suggests MASLD adds a distinct symptom burden on top of HBV itself, rather than simply reflecting older or sicker patients accumulating a second diagnosis. Because the Global Liver Registry enrolls patients across multiple countries, the consistency of this pattern across such a geographically diverse HBV population strengthens the case that the association is not a quirk of a single health system. In HCV, MASLD Skews Younger and More Often Female Among patients with HCV, those with MASLD were significantly younger and more frequently female than those without it (both P < .01), despite having similar rates of advanced fibrosis, biopsy-confirmed cirrhosis, and nonmetabolic comorbidities (all P > .05). They scored significantly lower on the FACIT-F Physical Well-Being domain and all CLDQ domains (all P < .01), with the steepest declines in the Systemic Symptoms and Worry domains, each also a 6% reduction across the scale's range. In multivariate analysis adjusting for other clinical factors, MASLD remained independently associated with lower CLDQ scores (P < .05). The researchers also relied on a validated noninvasive index rather than imaging or biopsy to define MASLD across thousands of patients, a practical tradeoff for a registry of this scale but one that leaves some misclassification possible. For clinicians, the findings argue for screening patients with chronic viral hepatitis for cardiometabolic risk factors rather than assuming stable fibrosis status means a stable symptom burden. The overall PCR-confirmed prevalence of HBV was 12.91%, while HCV prevalence was 7.04%, with the two viruses showing different patterns across the study settings. The study, published in BMC Infectious Diseases on 29 October 2026 as an open-access research article, was led by Awayimbo Ruth Jaggu and colleagues, with Adamu Ishaku Akyala as senior author. It recruited participants from three distinct settings in equal measure: a tertiary healthcare facility population at the Federal Medical Centre, Keffi, and two community-based populations in Akwanga and Lafia Local Government Areas, with 284 participants per setting. Participants completed structured questionnaires covering socio-demographic characteristics, behaviours, healthcare-related exposures, and household contacts. Screening used rapid diagnostic tests, followed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and polymerase chain reaction (PCR), which served as the reference standard for infection classification. Data were analysed with IBM SPSS Statistics version 26.0, using descriptive statistics, bivariate analysis with crude odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals, and multivariable logistic regression producing adjusted odds ratios, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. Discover more Biology textbook sales Study Biology hospital hospitals Learn Engineering HBV prevalence was 11.80% in community-based populations and 15.14% in the facility-based population. The researchers report no statistically significant difference in HBV prevalence between community and facility participants (χ2 = 1.86; p = 0.206), suggesting the virus circulates at similar levels in both contexts. HCV told a different story: prevalence was 5.28% in community populations but 10.56% among facility-based participants, a difference the authors report as statistically significant (χ2 = 7.028; p = 0.007). The multivariable analysis identified specific exposures independently associated with each virus. For HBV, sharing of personal hygiene items was associated with infection (adjusted odds ratio = 1.73; 95% CI: 1.06–2.70; p = 0.040), as was a history of sexually transmitted infections (AOR = 2.47; 95% CI: 1.38–4.42; p = 0.030). For HCV, a history of blood transfusion was independently associated with infection (AOR = 2.11; 95% CI: 1.04–4.31; p = 0.040). These associations come from a cross-sectional design, which measures exposures and infections at a single point in time. The adjusted odds ratios describe statistical associations rather than demonstrated causal effects, and the study’s findings apply to the adults sampled in these three Nasarawa State settings. The authors note that data on prevalence and associated risk factors across community- and facility-based populations in Nigeria, including Nasarawa State, have remained limited, which the study was designed to address. The higher HCV prevalence among facility-based participants coincided with the finding that blood transfusion history was independently associated with HCV infection, though the study did not test whether this or other healthcare-related exposures explain the difference between settings. Discover more Track Biotech Tour Colleges Genetic testing kits Health Laboratory supplies Chronic viral hepatitis due to HBV and HCV remains a significant global public health problem and a leading cause of liver-related morbidity and mortality, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, according to the study’s background. The authors conclude that both infections remain prevalent in community- and facility-based populations in Nasarawa State, and that the identified behavioural and healthcare-related exposures highlight the need for expanded vaccination programmes, routine hepatitis screening, community education, and strengthened infection prevention and control measures. The study was published as an early-share, peer-reviewed accepted article carrying a permanent DOI; the publishers note that this version is subject to further edits and will be replaced by the final Version of Record. The authors state that targeted, context-specific public health interventions are required to support prevention, early detection, and management of viral hepatitis, and to contribute to Nigeria’s 2030 viral hepatitis elimination goals. As a single-state cross-sectional survey of 852 adults, the findings describe the burden and associated factors in these specific populations rather than national estimates, and the reported prevalence figures should be read within that scope. The researchers also report that the prevalence and incidence rate of hepatitis B in the world and in China are decreasing year by year, and that China’s incidence is higher than the global average. The mortality rate among people aged 55 and above in China was reported to be lower than the global average. To model the data, the team established a series of time series and machine learning models. The comparison set included traditional approaches such as exponential smoothing, ARIMA and support vector regression, alongside individual machine learning models including convolutional neural networks, gated recurrent units and long short-term memory networks. The hybrid LSTM + CNN model achieved the strongest performance, with a coefficient of determination of 0.603. The authors state that this prediction performance was superior to the traditional time series models and the individual machine learning models tested. They also note that all of the time series models were able to capture the trend of the hepatitis B incidence rate. In their conclusions, the researchers write that the LSTM + CNN model demonstrates competitive performance in predicting the monthly average incidence rate of hepatitis B in China. They add that the hybrid deep learning model has shown great potential in time series prediction, although they emphasize that further validation is needed. The authors describe the work as a methodological exploration. They state that the study explores effective methods for predicting infectious disease time series and provides a new perspective for infectious disease prediction studies. The reported performance figure reflects the model’s fit within this study’s data and should be interpreted with the authors’ own caveat about the need for further validation. Hepatitis B remains an important public health issue facing China, according to the study’s background, and is described as one of the most severe infectious diseases in the world. The authors frame reliable incidence forecasting as a tool for early monitoring and early warning of infectious diseases, which is the stated motivation for comparing multiple modeling approaches in a single systematic analysis. The article was published as open access research on 08 October 2026, with Minquan Guan, Zhouying Hu, Yichen Lin, Xuehui Meng and Chengcheng Li among the listed authors. The study is presented as a methodological contribution to infectious disease modeling rather than a clinical intervention, and its findings concern statistical prediction of reported incidence rates rather than treatment or prevention outcomes. Pooling data from 117 studies identified through searches of eight academic databases covering 2016 to 2026, researchers led by Efosa Ekhator and colleagues estimated that 3.86 percent of internally displaced persons, refugees and asylum seekers are living with the viral infection, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 3.45 to 4.29 percent. Prevalence was markedly higher among men, at 5.98 percent (95 percent CI: 4.61 to 7.50 percent), than among women, at 3.82 percent (95 percent CI: 2.96 to 4.78 percent). Displaced people from Eastern Asia recorded the highest pooled prevalence, 11.62 percent (95 percent CI: 7.61 to 16.32 percent), followed by those from South-eastern Asia at 7.18 percent (95 percent CI: 5.70 to 8.80 percent) and Sub-Saharan Africa at 6.62 percent (95 percent CI: 5.44 to 7.90 percent). Displacement status itself appeared to matter. Internally displaced persons showed a pooled prevalence of 9.99 percent (95 percent CI: 6.82 to 13.67 percent), significantly higher than other subgroups at the p ≤ 0.05 threshold. People hosted in African countries had a pooled prevalence of 7.74 percent (95 percent CI: 5.02 to 10.97 percent), and those living in displacement camps recorded 7.19 percent (95 percent CI: 5.47 to 9.11 percent). Methodologically, the review screened 4,673 records and extracted data from each included study, assessing methodological quality with the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist. That heterogeneity proved substantial. Even after subgroup analyses, considerable variability remained across the included studies, and multivariate meta-regression linked it to several study-level characteristics: displacement status, the percentage of male participants, the temporal design of the studies and the settings in which they were conducted. This means the pooled estimates should be read as averages across widely differing populations, sampling strategies and screening approaches rather than as a single uniform prevalence figure applicable everywhere. The authors took several steps to probe the reliability of their results. A leave-one-out sensitivity analysis, which re-estimates the pooled prevalence while excluding each study in turn, demonstrated the robustness of the findings, indicating that no single study was driving the overall result. Publication bias, the tendency for smaller or less striking results to go unpublished, was assessed with Egger's regression test and funnel plot visualisation. The authors note that their estimates are subject to the limitations inherent in meta-analysis of observational prevalence studies, including the residual heterogeneity and the small-study effect detected by Egger's test. Even so, the consistency of the elevated burden across sensitivity analyses supports the paper's central conclusion that displaced populations represent a group with a high prevalence of hepatitis B and a corresponding claim on public health resources. Researchers assessed 320 patients from October 2023 through January 2024, combining structured questionnaires, physical examinations and medical-chart reviews. HBsAg positivity, indicating the presence of hepatitis B surface antigen, was identified in 134 participants, giving a prevalence of 41.9% with a 95% confidence interval of 36.5% to 47.5%. The hospital-based design establishes the burden among people already receiving care for chronic liver disease, but it does not show whether hepatitis B caused their underlying liver disease or how common infection is in the wider regional population. The study focused on patients with established chronic liver disease, a group described in the research as vulnerable to acute or superimposed hepatitis B infection. The authors noted that such infections can trigger rapid hepatic decompensation, accelerate progression toward cirrhosis and increase the lifetime risk of neoplastic transformation. Its primary result was the prevalence of HBsAg positivity and the statistical associations between this status and reported or recorded characteristics. Multivariable binary logistic regression identified several characteristics associated with positive HBsAg status. HIV-positive participants had three times the adjusted odds of positivity compared with HIV-negative patients, with an adjusted odds ratio of 3.00 and a 95% confidence interval of 1.40 to 6.80. A family history of liver disease was associated with 4.70 times the adjusted odds, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.90 to 11.00, while a history of dental procedures was associated with 4.50 times the adjusted odds, with a 95% confidence interval of 2.00 to 10.00. Contact with a person who had jaundice was also associated with higher odds of positivity, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.40 and a 95% confidence interval of 1.20 to 4.80. These are associations in the sampled population, not evidence that any listed exposure transmitted the virus. Because hepatitis B prevalence was high in the study population, the investigators also applied a modified Poisson regression model with robust variance to complement the odds-ratio estimates with adjusted prevalence ratios. In that model, HIV-positive status was associated with an adjusted prevalence ratio of 1.68, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.20 to 2.35. Family history of liver disease was associated with a ratio of 1.76, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.29 to 2.40. Contact with a jaundiced person had an adjusted prevalence ratio of 1.48, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.14 to 1.92, and a history of dental procedures had a ratio of 1.62, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.21 to 2.17. The logistic and modified Poisson analyses pointed in the same direction for these four predictors. Post-hoc power calculations indicated greater than 85% statistical power for the primary multivariable predictors. That calculation was performed after model fitting and does not eliminate uncertainties associated with the sample size, model specification, confounding or the cross-sectional design. In particular, the study cannot establish the timing or route of infection, determine whether identified characteristics preceded HBsAg positivity, or measure changes in prevalence over time. The referral-hospital setting also limits generalization: the participants were patients attending selected public facilities in Bahir Dar, rather than a population-based sample representing all people with chronic liver disease in Northwest Ethiopia. Within those limits, the 41.9% estimate documents a substantial hepatitis B burden among the chronically ill patients attending the three hospitals during the study period. The hospital sample included patients with chronic liver disease, so the result should not be presented as a regional prevalence estimate for the general population. Nor does the cross-sectional analysis demonstrate that HIV, family history, dental procedures or contact with a jaundiced person caused infection. The adjusted estimates identify groups with higher observed prevalence in this clinical setting, while their confidence intervals show the degree of precision around each association. The authors proposed that the results may inform regional planning for hepatitis B screening within liver clinics, evaluation of targeted adult vaccination strategies and stronger use of standard infection-control measures in health facilities. The immediate research contribution is instead a cross-sectional measurement of HBsAg prevalence and its reported correlates among 320 chronic liver disease patients in a defined Ethiopian hospital network. For interpreting the results, the study type and population are central. It was a facility-based, cross-sectional assessment conducted from October 2023 to January 2024, not a longitudinal study or a clinical trial. Its strongest supported conclusion is that hepatitis B infection was common among the sampled chronic liver disease patients, with HIV positivity, family history of liver disease, dental-procedure history and contact with a jaundiced person each associated with higher adjusted prevalence or odds of HBsAg positivity. Douyin videos received substantially more user engagement, but popularity was not consistently associated with higher quality, according to the analysis published in BMC Infectious Diseases. The researchers searched both platforms on March 10, 2026, using the Chinese translation of “hepatitis B Virus.” After applying inclusion and exclusion criteria, the final sample contained 174 videos, including 87 from each platform. The investigators extracted video characteristics such as duration, age, engagement metrics and uploader identity before evaluating the information presented in each video. Content quality and reliability were assessed with five instruments: the Global Quality Scale (GQS), the modified Decision-making Information Support Criteria for Evaluating the Reliability of Non-randomized Studies (mDISCERN), JAMA benchmark criteria, a Content Completeness Score (CCS) and the Video Information and Quality Index (VIQI). The statistical analysis included Mann–Whitney U tests, Kruskal–Wallis tests, Spearman correlation and multivariable regression, conducted in R version 4.3.2. Douyin videos attracted substantially greater engagement than Bilibili videos even after adjustment for video age. However, the study did not find a consistent relationship between engagement and superior content quality, indicating that user interaction could not serve as a dependable proxy for the quality of HBV-related videos. Bilibili videos were longer and scored significantly higher on three of the five assessment instruments: GQS, mDISCERN and VIQI. Discover more Check Symptoms Donate to Research Explore Data Study Biology Read Economics The reported P values for these differences were 0.027, 0.046 and below 0.001, respectively. These cross-sectional findings describe the selected videos and do not show that either platform inherently produces better material or that watching content from a particular platform improves viewers’ understanding of HBV. Multivariable analyses indicated that longer duration was independently associated with higher scores on all five quality measures, with all P values below 0.05. Platform was not independently associated with any quality measure after the other variables included in the models were considered. Video length was therefore the characteristic most consistently associated with higher assessed quality in this sample, rather than platform identity. The videos also differed in the clinical topics they addressed. records.content: Your Clinical Hub News & Perspective Tools & Reference CME/CE More Video Events Specialties Topics RegisterLog In Ask AI Search Medscape Medical NewsConference News Over Half of the Young Children Exposed to Household Hepatitis B Had an Infected Contact Other Than Their Mother Tara Haelle October 26, 2026 WASHINGTON — More than 1% of infants and young children lived in a household with someone who had an active hepatitis B infection, and over half of those infected household contacts were not their birth mother, according to a retrospective cohort study presented at IDWeek in Washington, DC, on October 22. “Maternal hepatitis B screening would not identify these exposures,” Karen B. Jacobson, MD, MPH, an infectious disease physician and research scientist with the Vaccine Study Center at the Kaiser Permanente Northern California (KPNC) Division of Research in Oakland, told attendees. “Some household-exposed infants did not receive a hepatitis B vaccine at birth and remained at risk for hepatitis B infection in the first months of life,” Jacobson said. “While most US children currently receive hepatitis B vaccine at birth, changes to vaccine policy may leave children at risk of hepatitis B transmission and chronic infection. Even if it is possible to accurately identify every single maternal infection, this would not account for potential exposure to an infected father, grandparent, or another person living in the household and, of course, anyone that they might come into close contact with outside the household.” A birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine protects infants before every possible exposure can be identified, she said, and avoids relying on whether close contacts or household members have been diagnosed with hepatitis B or are known to the family. “The key takeaway is that you can get hepatitis B from a source other than your mother in the first few years of life, at a time when you are most vulnerable,” Paul Offit, MD, an infectious disease pediatrician and director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia who was not involved in the study, said. “If you get hepatitis B in those first few years, you have a high rate of going on to develop cirrhosis or liver cancer later in life and limiting your lifespan. That makes it all the more important to get the hepatitis B vaccine.” An estimated 1-2 million people in the US have chronic hepatitis B infection, and infants can acquire hepatitis B via vertical transmission from their mothers during birth or from close interpersonal contact after birth, particularly from household contacts. Approximately 90% of infants who contract hepatitis B develop a chronic infection, but a birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine reduces risk for transmission by 85-95%. For that reason, the CDC has recommended vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B since 2005, an update from the 1991 recommendation to vaccinate infants at birth or within their first 2 months. But in December 2025, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), newly reconstituted by the US Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr, after he dismissed all the previous members, voted to change the recommendation. They recommended vaccinating newborns at birth only if their mothers had an active hepatitis B infection or unknown infection status and then offering the vaccine, with shared decision-making, to babies aged 2 months if their mothers were negative for hepatitis B. “This [recommendation] change sparked a lot of debate,” Jacobson said. “Many public health professionals and organizations voiced concerns that delayed vaccination would allow infants to fall through the cracks due to missed maternal infections or loss to follow-up. And furthermore, it does not take into account the risk of potential exposure from nonmaternal sources or close contacts of the infant.” The recommended change has currently been stayed by a federal judge due to an ongoing lawsuit between the American Academy of Pediatrics and Kennedy, but national discussion has continued over the risk of hepatitis B to unvaccinated infants in their first months of life. “Therefore, we sought to characterize household exposure to individuals with active hepatitis B infection among young children, including exposure through individuals who are not the birth mother,” Jacobson said. “In other words, is this a problem? Are there infants that could potentially be exposed either from the mother or from someone in their household during the weeks after birth, before most children go to daycare or school?” The researchers used data from the KPNC healthcare system, into which approximately 40,000 infants are delivered each year. The study population included all children younger than 5 years on June 16, 2023, whose record was linked to their birth mother and who lived with at least one household contact who used the KPNC. The researchers then tracked active hepatitis B infections among household contacts through March 26, 2026. Among 131,800 households, there were 158,169 children younger than 5 years and 363,070 household contacts with an average age of 31 years. The majority (98.7%) of children lived in homes without hepatitis B exposure, meaning neither their mothers nor any of their household contacts had an active infection. Only 0.5% of the households had an active hepatitis B infection. Among the 2024 (1.3%) children living in a household with an active hepatitis B exposure, 41.8% were exposed at birth to a mother with hepatitis B and the remaining 58.2% had been exposed to another household member with hepatitis B. “This demonstrates that potential household exposure to hepatitis B is not limited to just maternal infection,” Jacobson said. “So when you have RFK Jr’s fake ACIP saying that you should vaccinate high-risk children, which are the children who are passing through birth canal where there’s hepatitis B, but there is no no-risk child,” Offit said. “Everybody’s at some risk because you don’t know the infection status of everyone who comes in contact with your child. So why take the chance?” All the infants exposed to hepatitis B at birth had been vaccinated within 1 week of birth, but 4.2% of children exposed to hepatitis B in the household remained unvaccinated for more than 1 month after birth, and two household-exposed children were never vaccinated. Meanwhile, 86.7% of unexposed infants were vaccinated before they were 7 days old. “We also found that household-exposed children were more likely than unexposed children to be vaccinated, and this suggests that some families or healthcare providers did recognize the potential risk associated with household exposure,” Jacobson said. “However, there again were some of those household-exposed infants that did not receive any vaccination at birth or even ever, despite that potential exposure.” The researchers also looked at how many children were tested for hepatitis B, and although 95% of those exposed at birth had undergone testing, only 3.6% of household-exposed children were ever tested. “This is a potential gap in care for children who have a known household contact,” Jacobson said. Further, the exposure risk may be underestimated because this analysis did not capture household contacts with an undiagnosed infection, non-KPNC members, and close contacts outside the household. “Transmission of hepatitis B to children from nonmaternal sources is currently quite rare in the United States due to the high vaccination rates, but if rates decrease, more infants could be at risk,” Jacobson said. The research was funded by KPNC. The research tracked natural killer cell subsets and circulating cytokines in 27 patients treated with pegylated interferon-alpha together with nucleos(t)ide analogs, and found that those who achieved on-treatment HBsAg loss by week 48 differed measurably from those who did not. The study set out to characterize how NK cell phenotypes, receptor expression and cytokine profiles change during this combination regimen and how those changes relate to clinical outcomes. HBsAg loss remains a major challenge in chronic hepatitis B, and identifying immune signatures associated with treatment response could help clarify the mechanisms behind successful therapy. The 27 participants were stratified into two groups at week 48: an on-treatment HBsAg loss group, defined as HBsAg below 0.05 IU/mL, comprising 10 patients, and a non-HBsAg loss group of 17 patients. Flow cytometry was used to assess NK cell subsets, distinguishing CD56bright from CD56dim cells, and to measure expression of the receptors NKG2D, NKp30, NKp46, KIR, NKG2A and TIM3. Serum levels of the cytokines IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-2, IL-4, IL-6 and IL-10 were measured by ELISA, and the researchers analyzed correlations between virological markers and NK cell subsets, receptors or cytokines. Discover more Check Symptoms Book Lab Tests Study Biology Get Health Tips Across both groups, the combination therapy expanded CD56bright NK cells while reducing CD56dim subsets. The groups diverged in receptor expression. In the on-treatment HBsAg loss group, the researchers observed persistent upregulation of KIR, the killer cell immunoglobulin-like receptor, on CD56bright NK cells. At the same time, CD56dim NK cells in that group maintained elevated expression of NKG2A, a receptor that modulates NK cell activity. Cytokine patterns also separated the two groups. Patients in the on-treatment HBsAg loss group showed significantly lower serum levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-6 and IL-2, while maintaining higher levels of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10. This combination of dampened inflammatory signaling and preserved anti-inflammatory activity characterized the group that achieved HBsAg loss. Correlation analysis added another layer. In the on-treatment HBsAg loss group, HBsAg levels showed significant inverse correlations with the proportion of CD56bright NK cells and with receptor expression. In the same group, HBsAg correlated positively with CD56dim NK cell frequency. In both treatment groups, HBsAg was positively correlated with pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, linking viral antigen burden to inflammatory cytokine output. The authors conclude that PEG-IFNα and NAs combination therapy is associated with on-treatment HBsAg loss at week 48, potentially through optimizing cytokine responses, regulating the CD56bright to CD56dim NK cell balance and modulating the related receptors. The study notes limitations including its single-center design and moderate sample size, and the findings are observational associations rather than proof of causation. The work was registered in a national medical research registry under the title Prediction of clinical curative effect of pegylated interferon a individualized intermittent treatment of nucleoside (acid) in patients with hepatitis B, with registration number MR-53-26-076931, dated 31 August 2026. The study was published as open access on 12 October 2026, and the article version shared at publication is citable and carries a permanent DOI, subject to further edits before the final version of record appears. Using MAGPIX multiplex analysis, the researchers found that macrophage colony-stimulating factor, FLT-3 ligand, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, epidermal growth factor and transforming growth factor alpha had potential as diagnostic biomarkers. A decision-tree analysis indicated that combined detection of macrophage colony-stimulating factor and FLT-3 ligand was more valuable diagnostically than the individual measurements considered in that model. Occult hepatitis B infection, abbreviated OBI, is defined by the presence of hepatic hepatitis B virus DNA despite the absence of detectable serum hepatitis B surface antigen, or HBsAg. The study initially enrolled 6,773 healthy volunteers, with individuals under 18 excluded. Screening for hepatitis B markers then identified 57 cases of OBI. The comparison group comprised 37 donors selected from the same initial cohort who had no viral hepatitis markers, HIV or somatic diseases. The investigators measured cytokines, chemokines and growth factors in blood plasma to characterize the immune-mediator profile associated with occult infection. The group also showed elevated concentrations of six growth factors: epidermal growth factor, FLT-3 ligand, transforming growth factor alpha, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, macrophage colony-stimulating factor and vascular endothelial growth factor. The authors characterized occult hepatitis B as having a dominant anti-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic background, a profile they said could facilitate viral persistence and promote liver fibrosis. Receiver operating characteristic analyses indicated diagnostic potential for five measured mediators: macrophage colony-stimulating factor, FLT-3 ligand, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, epidermal growth factor and transforming growth factor alpha. The decision-tree results further supported measuring macrophage colony-stimulating factor together with FLT-3 ligand as a combined diagnostic approach. These findings represent associations and model-based estimates within the screened cohort, not proof of clinical performance in routine use. The supplied study abstract does not provide sensitivity, specificity, confidence intervals or independent validation, so the strength of the proposed biomarkers cannot be fully evaluated from the reported information alone. The authors interpreted the elevated growth-factor response as a feature of aberrant tissue repair. They linked transforming growth factor alpha and epidermal growth factor to incomplete regeneration and scarring, while the broader cytokine environment was described as favoring persistence of the virus. FLT-3 ligand appeared to have a potentially dual role, associated with hepatoprotection on one hand and fibrotic progression on the other. These are mechanistic interpretations of the observed pattern rather than demonstrated causal effects. The study was an observational comparison of circulating immune mediators, not a treatment trial or longitudinal analysis, so it does not establish that the measured cytokines preceded infection or fibrosis. Its strongest supported contribution is the identification of a blood-based cytokine and growth-factor pattern associated with occult hepatitis B, including a combination with potential diagnostic value that requires further validation. Yet the drug carries a well-recognized hematologic price: leukopenia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia are among its best-documented adverse effects and can shape treatment tolerability, monitoring intensity, dose decisions, and the need for supportive care. A new exploratory analysis, published in Frontiers in Medicine, has now tracked these blood count declines in detail within a small, prospectively followed cohort of 21 Chinese patients, quantifying how uniformly and how deeply counts fell during the first ten weeks of therapy, and asking whether the pattern differed between patients who showed an early serological response and those who did not. The study, conducted at the Second Affiliated Hospital and Yuying Children’s Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University between July 2024 and February 2025, enrolled adults with chronic hepatitis B who received peginterferon alfa-2b at 180 micrograms subcutaneously once weekly, with or without background oral nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy. The investigators classified patients operationally by early serological response through Week 15: among those with detectable hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) at baseline, response required either a decline of at least 1.0 log10 IU/mL from baseline or a fall of HBsAg below the assay’s lower limit of detection; among those already below that limit, response required anti-HBs seroconversion to at least 10 mIU/mL. Thirteen patients met response criteria and eight did not. Because the cohort size was set by the available parent study rather than by a formal sample-size calculation, the authors framed the entire analysis as hypothesis-generating. The central clinical finding was strikingly uniform. White blood cell count, absolute neutrophil count, and platelet count all declined from the first visit to the third visit in both response groups, and every single paired change was negative. Among the 13 responders, the median paired changes from Visit 1 to Visit 3 were −2.430 × 109/L for white blood cells (bootstrap 95% confidence interval: −2.530 to −1.530), −1.730 × 109/L for neutrophils (−1.990 to −1.094), and −67.0 × 109/L for platelets (−83.0 to −55.0), each with a matched-pairs rank-biserial correlation of −1.00. Among the 8 non-responders, the corresponding medians were −2.745 × 109/L for white cells (−3.570 to −2.190), −1.870 × 109/L for neutrophils (−2.260 to −1.110), and −97.5 × 109/L for platelets (−112.0 to −64.0). Visit 2 occurred at a median of 34 days after Visit 1, and Visit 3 at a median of 70 days, corresponding roughly to weeks 5 and 10 of treatment. Discover more Check Symptoms Book Lab Tests Study Biology Get Health Tips Find Treatments The observed nadirs told a similar story of broad, treatment-associated myelosuppression. Median white cell nadirs were 2.29 × 109/L in responders and 3.25 × 109/L in non-responders; median neutrophil nadirs were 1.10 and 1.69 × 109/L respectively; and median platelet nadirs were 86.0 and 112.0 × 109/L. However, when the investigators formally compared the two groups, the estimates were imprecise. The responder-minus-non-responder Hodges–Lehmann shift for white cell nadir was −0.810 × 109/L with a confidence interval spanning −1.240 to 0.160, and for neutrophil nadir −0.391 × 109/L (−0.830 to 0.330); the platelet nadir shift was −20.0 × 109/L (−39.0 to 7.0). None of these comparisons established a response-group-specific toxicity pattern, and the authors were careful to note that the wide intervals preclude any claim of equivalence between the groups as well. Binary thresholds underscored how common the cytopenias were. At Visit 2, white blood cell counts below 4.0 × 109/L occurred in 19 of 21 patients, or 90.5% (exact 95% confidence interval: 69.6% to 98.8%). Neutrophil counts below 1.0 × 109/L were seen in 7 of 21 patients (33.3%), and platelet counts below 100 × 109/L in 10 of 21 (47.6%). The near-universality of the white cell threshold led the team to treat it as a pragmatic clinical-management context rather than a discriminating molecular endpoint: when almost every patient crosses a cutoff, that cutoff carries little information for distinguishing molecular subgroups within the cohort. Discover more Seek Counseling Save on Rx Find Cancer Care A methodologically notable feature of the study was its handling of supportive care. Oral leukocyte-support medication was given to some patients after their counts fell, which raises the question of whether later blood counts reflect the drug’s toxicity or the mitigation of it. The team reconstructed treatment timing from deidentified records and built a post-documented oral-support-date indicator, classifying each complete blood count as before or after the first documented treatment date. In a random-intercept model covering 60 planned-visit observations from all 21 participants, the post-date term was −0.008 × 109/L for white cells (P = 0.979) and −0.105 × 109/L for neutrophils (P = 0.632), meaning the indicator did not materially alter the fitted decline. Boundary analyses coding ambiguous same-day visits as exposed or unexposed, and a strict pre-support paired set of five responders and four non-responders, all remained directionally consistent with decline. Crucially, because support was initiated in response to low counts, these non-randomized analyses cannot estimate treatment efficacy or remove confounding by indication. The second half of the study turned to whole-blood RNA sequencing, asking whether baseline host molecular state was associated with the hematologic endpoints. Blood samples collected in PAXgene tubes at Weeks 0, 5, and 10 were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform, and gene-level counts were normalized using the variance-stabilizing transformation in DESeq2. Hallmark pathway activity was summarized with gene set variation analysis across 50 pathways per endpoint family, with Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction applied within complete families. The result was a disciplined null: across 350 baseline associations in seven endpoint-specific families, no Hallmark pathway reached the prespecified exploratory threshold of q < 0.10, with a minimum q of 0.251. No baseline candidate-gene association met the threshold either (minimum q = 0.417). In paired Week-10-minus-Week-0 analyses among the 20 patients with both time points, none of 150 Hallmark associations reached q < 0.10. Because whole-blood expression reflects both cell-intrinsic transcription and shifts in circulating cell composition, the researchers ran a sensitivity analysis using xCell2, a reference-based tool that infers cell-type enrichment from bulk transcriptomes. The inferred neutrophil enrichment score showed only modest and imprecise concordance with measured neutrophil counts at baseline (Spearman rho = 0.382, confidence interval −0.110 to 0.732), but tracked measured counts much more strongly across matched visits (rho = 0.693 for neutrophils, 0.559 for white cells) and for within-person changes over time. Composition adjustment changed several pathway estimates, and a few adjusted platelet-endpoint signals nominally crossed q < 0.10, but none reached q < 0.05, four of seven had nonconverged confidence intervals, and the intervals were extremely wide. The authors declined to interpret these unstable signals as pathway discoveries, emphasizing that the enrichment scores are relative measures derived from the same bulk data as the pathway scores, leaving residual confounding and mathematical coupling as live concerns. The discussion places the findings in biological context without overclaiming mechanism. Type-I-interferon receptors and signaling have been demonstrated in CD34-positive hematopoietic progenitor cells, and interferon exposure can rapidly suppress hematopoiesis, supporting a marrow-production component for the leukocyte and neutrophil declines. For platelets, experimental type-I-interferon signaling can reduce platelet production and function, and prior small studies in chronic hepatitis B and other viral hepatitides have suggested impaired platelet production rather than antibody-mediated destruction. The authors note, however, that they did not measure bone-marrow function, endogenous G-CSF, antiplatelet antibodies, or thrombopoiesis in their own cohort, so these mechanisms remain contextual rather than demonstrated. The study’s limitations are substantial and openly stated. It is an exploratory secondary analysis of a single-center cohort of 21 participants with no independent validation; the between-group confidence intervals are wide; only one participant was HBeAg-positive, limiting generalization; and whole-blood transcriptomics cannot be read as liver-intrinsic biology. What the analysis delivers is a carefully quantified clinical picture: during peginterferon alfa-2b-based therapy for chronic hepatitis B, white cell, neutrophil, and platelet counts fell in every patient studied, the decline was not clearly modified by early serological response status, and a near-universal white cell threshold is more useful for clinical management than for molecular stratification. The transcriptomic null results, reported with complete multiplicity control, serve as a cautionary benchmark for future biomarker claims in this space, and the authors stress that all findings require confirmation in larger, independent, preferably multicenter cohorts with orthogonal measurements of cell composition and hematopoietic function. The study enrolled 178 participants divided into two groups. The HBV-positive cohort comprised 124 cases: 49 patients with HBV-associated hepatocellular carcinoma, 33 with HBV-related cirrhosis, and 42 with chronic hepatitis B. The HBV-negative control group included 54 individuals, consisting of 35 patients with non-HBV hepatocellular carcinoma and 19 with hepatic hemangioma. This design allowed the investigators to compare ORC1 expression across the spectrum of HBV-driven liver disease while controlling for cancer that arises without viral infection. ORC1 in liver tissue was detected by immunohistochemistry. In a subset of 17 HBV-HCC patients for whom serum samples were available, the researchers also measured circulating ORC1 by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Logistic regression was used to identify factors independently associated with high ORC1 expression, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were used to compare how well tissue ORC1, alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), and des-gamma-carboxy prothrombin (DCP) discriminated HBV-HCC from other disease states. The central finding was that tissue ORC1 was significantly upregulated in HBV-positive patients, and HBV infection itself was independently associated with high ORC1 expression, with a statistical significance of P<0.001. Expression followed a clear gradient across disease stages: ORC1 levels increased progressively from chronic hepatitis B to cirrhosis to hepatocellular carcinoma. This pattern suggests that ORC1 tracks the proliferative activity that intensifies as HBV-related liver disease advances toward cancer. Because AFP and DCP, the conventional biomarkers for hepatocellular carcinoma, have well-recognized limitations in detecting early-stage disease, the researchers tested whether ORC1 could add diagnostic value. Tissue ORC1 showed only moderate discrimination between HBV-HCC and HBV-related cirrhosis, with an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.64, and between HBV-HCC and chronic hepatitis B, with an AUC of 0.66. The serum measurements added a cautious note of interest. In the 17 HBV-HCC patients with available serum, tissue and serum ORC1 were moderately correlated, with a Spearman rank correlation coefficient of 0.554 (95% confidence interval 0.085 to 0.822, P=0.021). The wide confidence interval reflects the very small subset size, so the relationship between circulating and tissue ORC1 requires confirmation in much larger cohorts before any clinical use of serum ORC1 could be considered. Not every association held up. ORC1 expression was not significantly associated with tumor diameter (P>0.05), meaning that within the HCC group, larger tumors did not necessarily express more ORC1. This suggests that ORC1 reflects the proliferative state of the underlying liver disease rather than the physical size of an established tumor. For prognostic information, the team turned to external validation using TCGA-LIHC, the liver hepatocellular carcinoma dataset of The Cancer Genome Atlas. In that dataset, high ORC1 expression was associated with poorer overall survival, with a hazard ratio of 1.7 and P=0.0026. This independent cohort analysis supports the interpretation that elevated ORC1 marks a more aggressive disease course, although the survival analysis was performed in a public database cohort rather than in the Chinese patient cohort itself. The authors conclude that ORC1 upregulation is independently associated with HBV infection and increases with disease progression across HBV-related liver disease. They characterize ORC1 as primarily a proliferation- and progression-related marker rather than a stand-alone diagnostic biomarker, given its only moderate discrimination for HBV-HCC. The research focuses on CD3-positive CD56-positive NKT-like cells, which bridge features of T cells and natural killer cells and contribute to both antiviral defense and tumor immune surveillance. In patients whose serum HBV DNA exceeded 10,000 IU per milliliter, these cells displayed clear signs of hypofunction, raising questions about how chronic viral replication shapes antitumor immunity in the liver. The researchers found that TIGIT levels on peripheral blood NKT-like cells rose in parallel with HBV DNA concentration, so the higher a patient's viral load, the more TIGIT their NKT-like cells carried. Functionally, the high-HBV group's NKT-like cells secreted reduced amounts of antiviral effector cytokines, indicating that the cells were present but blunted in their ability to respond. To test whether TIGIT itself was responsible for the impaired activity rather than merely a marker of it, the team compared the behavior of TIGIT-positive and TIGIT-negative NKT-like cells within the same patients. The TIGIT-positive subset showed significantly lower immune activity, supporting the idea that expression of this receptor tracks with a functionally exhausted state rather than simply accompanying it. A second layer of the mechanism involves plasmacytoid dendritic cells, or pDCs, which present the ligand CD155 that engages TIGIT. In patients with high HBV DNA, CD155 expression on pDCs was markedly upregulated compared with HCC patients whose viral loads were low. The most direct evidence came from co-culture experiments in which NKT-like cells and pDCs from patients were grown together and stimulated with hepatitis B core antigen, the viral protein that NKT-like cells would normally recognize. When the investigators blocked the TIGIT pathway, the effector function of the patients' NKT-like cells was restored, demonstrating that the receptor-ligand interaction was actively suppressing the cells rather than simply correlating with their dysfunction. The new data provide a rationale for developing TIGIT-directed immunotherapy specifically for hepatocellular carcinoma patients with high HBV loads, a group whose disease is driven by both chronic viral infection and tumor progression. The clinical context matters. Persistent HBV infection can lead to chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis, and high serum HBV DNA is recognized as a major risk factor for the development of hepatocellular carcinoma. The study's scope should be kept in mind. The work examined peripheral blood cells rather than tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, and the functional restoration was demonstrated in co-culture assays rather than in patients. Whether TIGIT blockade would improve clinical outcomes in high-HBV HCC patients remains an open question that would require clinical testing. Nevertheless, by linking viral load, receptor expression, ligand upregulation, and reversible dysfunction in a single mechanistic chain, the study offers a coherent account of how chronic HBV replication may undermine one arm of antitumor immunity and identifies a concrete molecular target for future intervention. The audit, published in AIDS Research and Therapy as a Brief Communication, examined 183 patients with current or prior HBV exposure. Of these, 12 patients were switched to HBV-inactive antiretroviral therapy, meaning regimens that do not include drugs with activity against hepatitis B. According to the authors, there were significant variations in the testing practice performed before and after the switch to monitor potential HBV activity. This suggests that clinicians managing these patients did not follow a uniform approach to checking whether hepatitis B remained suppressed once HBV-active drugs were removed from the regimen. The authors note that consistency between guidelines would enhance implementation efforts in their context. The finding highlights a practical question raised by the study: how HBV-inactive antiretroviral therapy affects clinical monitoring in patients co-infected with HIV and HBV, and what optimal monitoring practices should be for HBV exposure in HIV patients on antiretroviral therapy. As an audit of clinical practice rather than an intervention study, the work describes what was observed at a single service setting and does not establish outcomes of any particular monitoring approach. The authors frame their conclusion around the need for greater guideline consistency to support implementation in their context.
